drills.q: What Next.js function marks a server-side function as callable directly from a Client Component?
Which of Next.js's four caching layers survives server restarts and is shared across different users' requests?
What Next.js function invalidates a tagged cache entry after a mutation?
A code reviewer approves a Server Action PR with no visible auth check, reasoning 'the UI already hides this button from unauthorized users.' What's wrong with this reasoning, in one sentence?
drills.a: UI-level hiding controls what renders, not what's callable -- a Server Action is a separately-callable public HTTP endpoint, discoverable in the client bundle, that anyone can invoke directly regardless of whether the associated button ever appears for them.

drills.q: A team updates a product's price via a Server Action, and the database write succeeds, but users keep seeing the old price for an extended period afterward. Diagnose.
drills.a: The mutation almost certainly forgot to call revalidateTag/revalidatePath after the write, leaving the persistent Data Cache serving the pre-mutation value to every subsequent reader -- mechanically the same bug class as forgetting to invalidate a Redis key after a database write in a traditional backend.

drills.q: Why does deploying database-querying code on the Edge runtime risk connection exhaustion under load, when the same code on the Node runtime typically doesn't?
drills.a: Edge executes in many short-lived, geographically distributed V8 isolates rather than a small number of long-running processes -- each ephemeral invocation opening its own raw connection (or contending for a small shared limit) is a structural mismatch with a traditional database's connection-count ceiling, unlike Node's ability to hold a real, properly-sized, long-lived connection pool.

drills.q: What was the key lesson from Next.js's July 2026 security release regarding where authorization checks should live?
drills.a: Real authorization checks must live inside Server Actions and Route Handlers themselves, not rely solely on middleware.ts/proxy.ts -- one of the nine disclosed vulnerabilities was specifically a middleware authorization bypass, showing middleware-only enforcement is insufficient as the sole defense layer.

drills.q: Design the caching strategy for a product page with three data elements of different freshness needs: static product description, occasionally-changing sale price, and frequently-changing live inventory count.
drills.a: Product description: Full Route Cache or long-TTL Data Cache, invalidated via revalidateTag only on admin edit. Sale price: Data Cache with a shorter TTL or explicit tag-based invalidation tied to the pricing-update mutation, since stale pricing has real business consequences. Live inventory: too high-frequency for cost-effective tag-based invalidation -- better served by making that specific fetch genuinely dynamic (excluded from persistent caching) or streamed/polled client-side.

drills.q: A Next.js Server Action deployed on the Edge runtime starts failing with database connection errors under moderate production load. Propose two fixes at two different levels of architectural change, and explain the decision criterion for choosing between them.
drills.a: Smaller fix: add a serverless/edge-aware connection-pooling proxy between edge invocations and the database, keeping the architecture otherwise unchanged -- appropriate under time pressure or for a genuinely small app with no other data consumers. Larger fix: extract a real backend service (on a traditional runtime with its own managed connection pool) that Next.js calls instead of touching the database directly, converting Next.js to a BFF role -- appropriate once multiple consumers need the same data, review discipline for inline DB access is a concern, or this incident is one of a recurring pattern rather than a one-off.

drills.q: When would you choose a Route Handler over a Server Action for a new Next.js endpoint, and give a concrete example where a Server Action would NOT work.
drills.a: Choose a Route Handler when the caller isn't your own React component tree -- a webhook receiver, mobile app, or third-party integration needs a stable, documented URL to call. Example: a payment provider's webhook notifying your app of a completed charge needs a Route Handler at a fixed endpoint; a Server Action relies on Next.js's internal client-to-server calling convention that an external system has no way to invoke.
